newsitem.title: USA: Eating disorders aggravate diabetes, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Eating disorders aggravate diabetes, study finds.

text.p: Eating disorders are common among teen-age girls suffering from diabetes and may cause eye problems for them later in life, according to a study released Wednesday.

In a survey of 91 young women between the ages of 12 and 18 who took insulin to treat diabetes, nearly a third of them admitted using laxatives, making themselves vomit, eating in binges or avoiding insulin use to keep their weight down.
Lead researcher Anne Rydall of Toronto Hospital and her colleagues concluded that eating disorders are "common and persistent" in young women with diabetes.
For many women, the problem persisted for years, according to the study, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
When the researchers re-examined the young women four to five years later, one-third still had behaviors indicating a moderate or severe eating disorder.
But the number of women who stopped or reduced insulin use in an effort to keep their weight down rose to 34 percent by the follow-up examination from 14 percent at the beginning of the study.

In an editorial in the journal, Drs. Gareth Williams and Geoffrey Gill of Fazakerley Hospital in Liverpool, England, said the study suggested that it is possible to change the behavior of young diabetic women with an eating disorder.
Many women with an eating disorder at the beginning of the study had apparently adopted healthy eating habits and proper insulin use five years later, they said.

They said that the study "focuses attention on the thorny problem of eating disorders, which are undoubtedly common in women with insulin-dependent diabetes and must be considered whenever diabetes proves difficult to control."

The most striking finding of the study, the researchers said, was the damage the improper eating behaviors had on the blood vessels around the girls' eyes, a complication of diabetes known as retinopathy, which can lead to blindness.

"Our study suggests that routine screening for eating disturbances may be (useful) in young women with diabetes and that some intervention should be undertaken, if eating disorders are detected, to minimize the risk of later complications," the researchers said.
